claim: Golden datasets should be version-controlled with every schema and label change tracked, and maintenance planned from day one by versioning prompts, datasets, and graders alongside a changelog.
quote: Version control the dataset; track every schema and label change... Plan for maintenance from day one. Version prompts, datasets, and graders; keep a changelog for schemas and rubrics.

claim: Practitioners should favor small, frequent updates over rare giant refreshes, pulling fresh scenarios from production logs and SME tickets and re-labeling high-impact slices.
quote: Favor small, frequent updates over rare, giant refreshes. Pull fresh scenarios from production, then re-label high-impact slices.

claim: A rubric change can falsely masquerade as a model win, so historical baselines must be protected when graders are updated.
quote: Statsig's Offline Evals make it easy to protect historical baselines so a rubric change does not masquerade as a model win.

claim: Error analysis should be re-run on significant changes (new features, prompt updates, model switches, bug fixes), reviewing 100+ fresh traces per cycle and 10-20 traces weekly between cycles.
quote: when making significant changes: new features, prompt updates, model switches, or major bug fixes... at least 100+ fresh traces each review cycle... review 10-20 traces weekly, focusing on outliers.

claim: An artificially high pass rate signals a weak eval; a 70% pass rate can indicate a more meaningful evaluation that actually stress-tests the application rather than being tuned to look good.
quote: a 70% pass rate might indicate a more meaningful evaluation that's actually stress-testing your application

claim: Goodhart's law (when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure) applies to LLM benchmarks: once labs treat a leaderboard ranking as the target metric, the metric loses validity.
quote: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure... once model labs began treating Arena ranking as the target metric, the metrics lost validity

claim: Selective disclosure gamed Arena scores: a modest increase in access to Arena data could boost a model's performance by up to 112%, and Meta tested 27 private variants before Llama-4, disclosing only the best.
quote: even a modest increase in access to Arena data could boost a model's Arena performance by up to 112%... 27 private LLM variants tested...in the lead-up to the Llama-4 release

claim: To prevent an LLM judge from memorizing answers, practitioners partition data and measure how well the judge generalizes to unfamiliar held-out data, targeting high true positive and true negative rates on a held-out labeled test set.
quote: avoid your LLM judge memorizing answers by partitioning your data and measuring how well the judge generalizes to unfamiliar data

claim: A common anti-pattern is treating custom evaluation as a one-time task with static offline datasets that quickly become outdated; dataset drift requires the eval set to shift as user behavior evolves.
quote: custom evaluation as a one-time task, relying on static offline datasets that quickly become outdated... Dataset Drift... your evaluation dataset must accompany this shift

claim: Benchmark saturation and data contamination inflate scores so high leaderboard numbers reflect overfitting to the benchmark rather than genuine real-world capability.
quote: benchmark saturation... overfitting to the benchmark rather than genuine improvements in real-world capability... data contamination, where models have seen parts of the test set during training, artificially inflating their scores

claim: Results from a single run or small dataset may not reflect true performance, and LLM judges carry systematic biases such as favoring LLM-generated over human-written text.
quote: results from a single run or a small dataset may not reflect true performance... systematic biases, such as favoring LLM-generated outputs over high-quality human-written text

claim: Shankar et al. identify criteria drift: users need criteria to grade outputs but grading outputs helps them define criteria, so a priori rubrics become misaligned as users refine standards on observing real outputs, undermining static eval sets.
quote: users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria
